cases.article: AHA 2025 Guidelines for CPR and ECC — Adult Advanced Life Support
cases.title: Witnessed collapse at the gym
cases.chiefComplaint: 58-year-old man, witnessed collapse, CPR in progress on arrival
cases.diagnosis: Ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest from acute coronary occlusion
cases.context: Witnessed arrest on a treadmill twenty minutes ago. A trainer started compressions within seconds and EMS took over four minutes later; the first analysed rhythm was coarse VF and no shock has been delivered — their monitor's battery failed and the replacement pads went on in the ambulance bay. He is 58, runs three times a week, on no medications. His wife is in the waiting room. Weight about 82 kg.
criticalActions: Provide high-quality compressions with a chest compression fraction of at least 80%
Defibrillate the shockable rhythm immediately and again every two minutes
Give epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes
Give an antiarrhythmic — amiodarone 300 mg or lidocaine 1-1.5 mg/kg — for refractory VF
Secure the airway and confirm it with waveform capnography
Search for and treat the reversible causes (Hs and Ts)
After ROSC obtain a 12-lead ECG and activate the cath lab for the occlusion
Start post-arrest care including targeted temperature management for a comatose survivor
learningPoints: In witnessed VF, defibrillation is the only intervention that terminates the rhythm — compressions and drugs buy time until the next shock, they do not convert it.
Biphasic energy is 120-200 J for the first shock (the manufacturer's recommendation), then equal or escalating energy up to 360 J.
Epinephrine 1 mg every 3-5 minutes throughout; in a shockable rhythm give it after the second shock rather than first, so defibrillation is never delayed for a drug.
Amiodarone 300 mg IV/IO (then 150 mg) or lidocaine 1-1.5 mg/kg for VF that persists after three shocks.
Chest compression fraction should be at least 80% — every pause for a pulse check, an intubation or a drug is a pause in coronary perfusion, so keep them under ten seconds.
Waveform capnography does three jobs at once: it confirms the tube, it grades compressions (aim above 10 mmHg), and an abrupt rise above 35 mmHg announces ROSC before anyone finds a pulse.
A sudden VF arrest in a middle-aged adult is coronary occlusion until proven otherwise — the 12-lead and the cath lab are part of the resuscitation, not the paperwork afterwards.
cases.intro: The medics wheel in a 58-year-old man who went down on a treadmill twenty minutes ago. One of them is on his chest, counting out loud; the other is squeezing a bag. The monitor above the trolley shows a coarse, chaotic trace with no organised complexes in it. The pads are on and connected to your defibrillator, and nobody has shocked him yet.

speech.speaker: medic
speech.text: Witnessed arrest at the gym, bystander CPR from the second he went down. Same trace the whole way in — our monitor died and the spare pads only went on two minutes ago, so he has had no shocks. He's about eighty kilos.

cases.title: Pulseless after a bedside procedure
cases.chiefComplaint: 44-year-old man, arrested minutes after a central line attempt
cases.diagnosis: Tension pneumothorax causing pulseless electrical activity after a right subclavian line attempt
cases.context: 44-year-old admitted from the ED with severe gallstone pancreatitis. He needed central access for pressors and the senior resident took three passes at a RIGHT SUBCLAVIAN line. Within four minutes he desaturated, went hypotensive and lost his pulse. The monitor shows a slow, wide, organised complex at about 34 with nothing at the femoral: PULSELESS ELECTRICAL ACTIVITY. True cause is a RIGHT TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX from the line attempt. CORRECT PATH: high-quality compressions, epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO immediately and every 3-5 minutes, no defibrillation (PEA is not shockable), immediate needle or finger decompression of the right chest, bag-mask or advanced airway with waveform capnography, then ROSC at the next rhythm check; chest tube once perfusing, then ICU. RED HERRINGS: reaching for the defibrillator, hunting for a pulse instead of decompressing, waiting for a chest film to confirm what the exam already says. DETERIORATION: undecompressed PEA degenerates to asystole at about ten minutes.
criticalActions: Start high-quality compressions immediately and keep the compression fraction above 80%
Give epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO straight away and repeat it every 3-5 minutes
Recognise the organised rhythm with no pulse as PEA and withhold defibrillation
Work the Hs and Ts out loud and name the cause this procedure can create
Decompress the chest on the side of the line attempt with a needle or finger thoracostomy
Ventilate and confirm the airway and CPR quality with waveform capnography
Place a definitive chest tube once there is a pulse and confirm it on a chest film
Admit to the ICU for post-arrest care with a 12-lead ECG and temperature management if he stays comatose
learningPoints: PEA is not a shockable rhythm: compressions plus epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes start at once, and a shock delivered into PEA only buys an interruption in perfusion and a burn.

In a non-shockable arrest the first dose of epinephrine goes in as early as possible — earlier administration is associated with better survival, and the repeat interval is 3-5 minutes, not whenever someone remembers.

PEA within minutes of a subclavian or internal jugular puncture is a tension pneumothorax until the chest has been decompressed; this is what the Hs and Ts are for in the first two minutes, not the tenth.

Needle decompression goes into the 4th or 5th intercostal space in the anterior axillary line (or the 2nd space mid-clavicular) with a catheter at least 5 cm long — the standard 3.2 cm cannula fails to reach the pleural space in most adults.
A needle is a temporising measure with a real failure rate: finger thoracostomy is the more reliable decompression during CPR, and a chest tube follows once there is a pulse.
Waveform capnography above 10 mmHg says the compressions are generating flow, and an abrupt rise above 35 mmHg announces ROSC — usually before anyone has a finger on a femoral.
Once the pressure is off the mediastinum the pulse returns at the next rhythm check, so reassess on the two-minute boundary instead of stopping compressions to hunt for it.

Compressions are running. The monitor shows a slow, wide, organised rhythm at about 34 — complexes on the screen, nothing under your fingers.

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: He's got complexes on the monitor and no pulse — I'm on the chest. He went off right after the line attempt.

speech.speaker: consultant
speech.text: Three passes on the right subclavian. I got a flash, then he desaturated and crashed. I never got the wire in.

cases.title: Found unresponsive behind a bus shelter
cases.chiefComplaint: 31-year-old woman found down, no pulse on arrival
cases.diagnosis: Opioid-associated cardiac arrest — asystole from prolonged respiratory arrest (illicit fentanyl)
cases.context: 31-year-old found unresponsive behind a bus shelter. A witness saw her sitting up fifteen minutes earlier. Medics found her apneic with pinpoint pupils and fresh track marks in both antecubital fossae; the initial monitor picture was agonal and by arrival it is ASYSTOLE. True scenario is an OPIOID-ASSOCIATED CARDIAC ARREST: the primary insult is respiratory, and the heart stopped because it ran out of oxygen. CORRECT PATH: confirm asystole in more than one lead, high-quality compressions, effective ventilation (bag-mask with an oral airway at 10 breaths a minute, then an advanced airway), epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO immediately and every 3-5 minutes, naloxone 2 mg IV/IO/IM, waveform capnography, and a glucose. ROSC follows once she has been oxygenated, given epinephrine and reversed. RED HERRINGS: defibrillating asystole; giving naloxone INSTEAD of ventilating; treating the arrest as primarily cardiac. DETERIORATION: without ventilation, epinephrine and reversal she is dead at twenty minutes.
criticalActions: Confirm asystole in more than one lead, keep compressions going and do not defibrillate
Ventilate effectively — bag-mask with an oral airway at 10 breaths per minute, then an advanced airway
Give epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO immediately and repeat it every 3-5 minutes
Give naloxone 2 mg IV/IO/IM for the suspected opioid arrest
Confirm the airway and CPR quality with waveform capnography
Check a bedside glucose and work the rest of the Hs and Ts
After ROSC keep her ventilated and monitored for re-sedation, and admit to the ICU
learningPoints: An opioid arrest is a respiratory arrest that has gone on too long: oxygen and ventilation are the treatment, and naloxone is an adjunct that does nothing for a patient nobody is ventilating.

Asystole and PEA are non-shockable. Confirm asystole in a second lead and check the leads and gain before you accept a flat line, then give epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO as early as you can and every 3-5 minutes.
Naloxone in cardiac arrest is 2 mg IV/IO/IM (4 mg intranasal), repeatable — the 0.4 mg titration is for the patient who is still breathing and whom you do not want to send into withdrawal.

Compressions run at 100-120 a minute, 5-6 cm deep, with full recoil and asynchronous ventilation at 10 breaths a minute once an advanced airway is in — hyperventilation raises intrathoracic pressure and lowers the pressure that fills the heart.
Waveform capnography confirms the tube, tracks CPR quality (aim above 10 mmHg) and announces ROSC with an abrupt rise above 35 mmHg.
Fentanyl and its analogues outlast naloxone, whose effect fades in 30-90 minutes — anyone reversed after an arrest is watched in a monitored bed, not discharged from the resus room.
Every opioid overdose survivor leaves with take-home naloxone and a warm handover to addiction services; the arrest you just reversed is the strongest predictor of the next one.

The medics were bagging her on the way in; the monitor shows a flat line and there is no pulse.

speech.speaker: medic
speech.text: Found her slumped, not breathing, pinpoint pupils. She was agonal when we got there and flatlined in the truck. We've been bagging and compressing, no drugs given.

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: Nothing on the monitor in two leads. Compressions are mine — tell me what you want.

cases.title: Repeated collapse at home
cases.chiefComplaint: 76-year-old woman, two blackouts today, grey and clammy on the trolley
cases.diagnosis: Third-degree (complete) atrioventricular block with a wide escape rhythm and shock
cases.context: 76-year-old brought in by her daughter after two syncopal episodes at home. She is AWAKE but grey, clammy and confused at the edges. The monitor shows a wide escape at 32 with P waves marching independently through the QRS complexes: COMPLETE HEART BLOCK. Systolic 70. She is not in arrest and must not be allowed to get there. Her daughter mentions a new tablet from the GP (metoprolol) — a red herring: the block is infranodal and will not lift with drug withdrawal in this timeframe. CORRECT PATH: pads on, oxygen if hypoxic, IV access, 12-lead, name the bradycardia UNSTABLE, atropine 1 mg IV (accepted, honest answer: no change — atropine does not work on infranodal block and must not delay pacing), then TRANSCUTANEOUS PACING with confirmed electrical AND mechanical capture, sedation and analgesia once capturing, or an epinephrine infusion 2-10 mcg/min if pacing fails. Cardiology for a transvenous wire, CCU. DETERIORATION: untreated she arrests into PEA at about eight minutes.
criticalActions: Put on pads, get IV access and oxygen, and take a 12-lead while you assess her perfusion
Name the bradycardia unstable — hypotension and syncope are perfusion failure, not a rate to observe
Give atropine 1 mg IV, repeatable every 3-5 minutes to a total of 3 mg, without letting it delay pacing
Start transcutaneous pacing and confirm both electrical and mechanical capture
Give sedation and analgesia once the pacer is capturing
Start an epinephrine infusion at 2-10 mcg/min (or dopamine 5-20 mcg/kg/min) if pacing fails or is unavailable
Look for a reversible cause — nodal blocking drugs, hyperkalaemia, ischaemia
Call cardiology for a transvenous wire and admit to the coronary care unit
learningPoints: A bradycardia is unstable when it is causing hypotension, altered mental status, shock, ischaemic chest pain or acute heart failure — the number on the monitor is not the diagnosis, the perfusion is.
Atropine is 1 mg IV, repeated every 3-5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg. The old 0.5 mg dose is gone, and doses below 0.5 mg can paradoxically slow the heart further.
Atropine works on the AV node, so it does almost nothing in high-degree block with a wide escape — give it while the pacer is being set up, never instead of setting it up.

Transcutaneous pacing needs both kinds of capture: a wide QRS with a T wave after every spike on the monitor, and a pulse or arterial trace that matches the paced rate. A pacer that is not capturing is a pacer that is not working.
Pacing hurts. An awake patient who is capturing needs analgesia and sedation, titrated so as not to lose the pressure you have just bought.
The alternatives to pacing are chronotropic infusions: epinephrine 2-10 mcg/min or dopamine 5-20 mcg/kg/min, titrated to perfusion, not to a target rate.

Transcutaneous pacing is a bridge measured in minutes to hours — a complete block with syncope needs a transvenous wire and a permanent pacemaker, so cardiology is called at the same time as the pacer goes on.
cases.intro: A 76-year-old woman is wheeled into resus by her daughter after two blackouts at home — the second one in the car park. She is awake and answering you, but she is grey, clammy and cold to the elbows, and she keeps saying the lights are going out. The monitor shows a wide, slow complex at 32 with P waves that have nothing to do with it, and the cuff reads 70 over 44.

speech.speaker: patient
speech.text: It goes dark... and then I'm on the floor. I can hear you, I just can't... hold on to anything.

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: Rate's 32, pressure 70 over 44, sats 93 on room air. Pads are on the trolley if you want them — say the word.

speech.speaker: family
speech.text: She's been slowing down all week. The doctor started her on a new tablet for her blood pressure on Monday.

cases.title: Palpitations that turned into chest pain
cases.chiefComplaint: 63-year-old man, racing heart for three hours, now grey and sweating
cases.diagnosis: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response causing haemodynamic instability
cases.context: 63-year-old, three hours of palpitations that began while he was mowing the lawn, now with crushing central chest pressure. He is IRREGULARLY IRREGULAR at about 170 with a systolic of 78, cold peripheries and a rising lactate: ATRIAL FIBRILLATION WITH RVR causing shock. CORRECT PATH: pads and monitor, IV access, 12-lead, name the tachycardia UNSTABLE, sedate if time allows, then SYNCHRONISED cardioversion at 120-200 J biphasic, escalating if the first attempt fails. ADENOSINE IS WRONG HERE and must be flagged: it does nothing for atrial fibrillation and is dangerous in pre-excited AF. Rate-control drugs (diltiazem, metoprolol) in a shocked patient will make the pressure worse. RED HERRINGS: adenosine, diltiazem, waiting for the troponin. DETERIORATION: untreated the ischaemia and the rate feed each other and he arrests into VF at about nine minutes.
criticalActions: Attach pads and the monitor, get IV access and a 12-lead while you assess perfusion
Name the tachycardia unstable — hypotension with ischaemic chest pain and poor perfusion
Sedate the awake patient before cardioverting if time allows
Deliver synchronised cardioversion at 120-200 J biphasic, escalating if the first shock fails
Keep adenosine and AV nodal blockers away from an irregularly irregular tachycardia in shock
Look for the driver — ischaemia, sepsis, thyrotoxicosis, pulmonary embolism, alcohol, electrolytes
Make the anticoagulation decision after conversion and admit to a monitored bed
learningPoints: Unstable means hypotension, altered mental status, signs of shock, ischaemic chest pain or acute heart failure caused by the rate — any one of them takes you straight to synchronised cardioversion.

Biphasic synchronised cardioversion for atrial fibrillation is 120-200 J; atrial flutter and regular narrow tachycardias take 50-100 J, and a regular wide-complex tachycardia takes 100 J. Escalate stepwise if the first attempt fails.

Synchronised means the shock lands on the R wave. An unsynchronised shock delivered in the vulnerable period of the T wave can induce ventricular fibrillation — press SYNC, see the markers on the R waves, then charge.

Sedate the awake patient before you cardiovert if the pressure and the clock allow it; a short-acting agent titrated in small doses is standard, and being in a hurry is not a reason to shock someone awake without trying.

Adenosine is for regular narrow-complex tachycardia. It will not convert atrial fibrillation, and in pre-excited AF it can accelerate conduction down an accessory pathway and precipitate ventricular fibrillation.
Diltiazem and metoprolol are for rate control in a patient who is perfusing. In a shocked patient their negative inotropy takes away the pressure you still have.

New atrial fibrillation in a 63-year-old with chest pain is a symptom, not the whole diagnosis: check for ischaemia, sepsis, thyrotoxicosis, pulmonary embolism and electrolyte disturbance once the rhythm is fixed.
cases.intro: A 63-year-old man is brought straight into resus by triage. His heart started racing three hours ago while he was mowing the lawn, and in the last twenty minutes it has turned into a crushing pressure across his chest. He is grey, wet with sweat, and his hands are cold. The monitor shows a narrow, irregularly irregular tachycardia at about 170, and the cuff reads 78 over 52.

speech.speaker: patient

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: 170 and all over the place, 78 systolic, sats 94. He's clammy as anything. Pads are in my hand, Doctor.

cases.title: Palpitations that started out of nowhere
cases.chiefComplaint: 29-year-old woman, heart racing for an hour, walked in talking
cases.diagnosis: Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia), haemodynamically stable
cases.context: 29-year-old who felt her heart 'flip' an hour ago and has been racing since. She walked into triage, she is talking in full sentences, her pressure is 112 systolic and she has no chest pain. The monitor shows a REGULAR NARROW tachycardia at 190 with no visible P waves: SUPRAVENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA, and she is STABLE. CORRECT PATH: monitor and pads, IV access, 12-lead, confirm regular and narrow, MODIFIED VALSALVA first (no change in this case), then ADENOSINE 6 mg rapid push with a flush (no change), then ADENOSINE 12 mg, which converts her. Electricity is for the unstable patient or for drug failure, and then only SYNCHRONISED and after sedation. RED HERRING: an UNSYNCHRONISED shock on a talking patient — the script accepts and delivers it and the debrief calls it what it is. DETERIORATION: left untreated for fifteen minutes she becomes unstable, and much later she arrests; she does not simply sit there at 190 forever.
criticalActions: Attach the monitor and pads, get IV access and a 12-lead, and confirm she is haemodynamically stable
Confirm the tachycardia is regular and narrow before you treat it
Try a vagal manoeuvre first — a modified Valsalva with leg elevation
Give adenosine 6 mg by rapid IV push with a 20 mL flush, then 12 mg if the first dose fails
Reserve electricity for instability or drug failure, and then only synchronised and after sedation
Look for the trigger and check electrolytes, thyroid function and a pregnancy test
Record a 12-lead after conversion and arrange follow-up before she goes home
learningPoints: Stable means she is perfusing: talking, no chest pain, no heart failure, a systolic of 112. A stable regular narrow tachycardia is treated with vagal manoeuvres and adenosine, not electricity.
The modified Valsalva — 15 seconds of strain, then supine with the legs raised to 45 degrees for 15 seconds — converts about 43% of episodes, roughly three times the standard technique.
Adenosine is 6 mg IV then 12 mg, pushed as fast as you can into a large proximal vein and chased immediately with 20 mL of saline: its half-life is under ten seconds, so a slow push is a wasted dose.
Warn her before you push it. A few seconds of chest pressure, flushing and a feeling of doom is expected, and the pause on the monitor is the drug working, not the patient arresting.

An unsynchronised shock on a patient with a pulse can land in the T wave and induce ventricular fibrillation. If a stable patient needs electricity because the drugs failed, sedate first and press SYNC — 50-100 J biphasic for a regular narrow tachycardia.

Adenosine is not for an irregular tachycardia. Hold it if the rhythm is irregular or the complexes are wide and pre-excitation is possible, and take a 12-lead during the conversion — the strip is diagnostic and nobody can get it back afterwards.
Check potassium, magnesium, thyroid function and a pregnancy test before she goes home, and refer recurrent episodes for electrophysiology study and ablation, which is curative in over 95% of AVNRT.
cases.intro: A 29-year-old woman walks into triage holding her chest, not because it hurts but because she can feel her heart going. It started an hour ago while she was sitting at her desk. She is talking to you in full sentences, warm and pink, pressure 112 over 74. The monitor shows a fast, regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 190 with no P waves anywhere.

speech.speaker: patient
speech.text: It just went — like a switch. It's done it before but never this long. Am I having a heart attack?

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: 190, regular as a metronome, 112 over 74, sats 99. She's completely with us. Pads are on the trolley if you want them on.

cases.title: Blackouts that keep coming back
cases.chiefComplaint: 52-year-old woman, three collapses today, unresponsive again in front of you
cases.diagnosis: Torsades de pointes from acquired long QT — methadone and ondansetron with hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia
cases.context: 52-year-old on a methadone programme, treated for two days with ondansetron for vomiting from a gastroenteritis, and dry from it. Three collapses today, each self-terminating. The medics' strip between runs shows a QT they measured at 610 ms with frequent ventricular ectopics landing on the T wave. On your trolley she goes into a POLYMORPHIC VENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA that twists around the baseline — TORSADES DE POINTES — and this run is not stopping: she has NO PULSE. CORRECT PATH: compressions, treat the pulseless polymorphic run as shockable and DEFIBRILLATE UNSYNCHRONISED at 200 J (sync cannot track a polymorphic QRS), MAGNESIUM SULFATE 2 g IV/IO, which is the treatment that actually stops the runs recurring, potassium to the high-normal range, and STOP every QT-prolonging drug. AMIODARONE IS WRONG and is flagged: it prolongs the QT further. If the runs keep recurring, overdrive pacing at 90-110 or an isoprenaline infusion shortens the QT. DETERIORATION: untreated the torsades degenerates into ventricular fibrillation at five minutes.
criticalActions: Start high-quality compressions and defibrillate the pulseless polymorphic run unsynchronised at 200 J
Give magnesium sulfate 2 g IV/IO over 1-2 minutes and repeat it if the runs continue
Measure the QT between runs and name the rhythm as polymorphic, not monomorphic, VT
Replace potassium to 4.5-5.0 mmol/L and give magnesium even when the level is normal
Stop every QT-prolonging drug she is on and give no further QT-prolonging antiarrhythmic
Ventilate and confirm the airway and CPR quality with waveform capnography
Arrange overdrive pacing at 90-110 or an isoprenaline infusion if the runs recur despite magnesium
Admit to coronary care with continuous QT monitoring and cardiology review
learningPoints: Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV/IO over 1-2 minutes is the treatment for torsades and works whether or not the magnesium level is low; it suppresses the early afterdepolarisations that trigger the runs without shortening the QT itself.

A polymorphic run with no pulse is defibrillated, unsynchronised, at the same energy as VF (120-200 J biphasic first, up to 360 J) — the defibrillator cannot synchronise to a QRS that changes shape every beat, and pressing SYNC will simply stop it firing.
Defibrillation stops the run in front of you; it does nothing about the substrate. Without magnesium and QT correction the torsades comes straight back, and each recurrence is another arrest.
Amiodarone, procainamide and sotalol all prolong the QT — giving them here is pouring petrol on the fire. Lidocaine is the antiarrhythmic that does not prolong the QT if one is truly needed.
Push the potassium up to 4.5-5.0 mmol/L: at a normal-but-low level the repolarisation reserve is still thin, and the runs keep coming.

Every QT-prolonging drug stops — here methadone and ondansetron together, a combination that is easy to prescribe and easy to miss. A QTc above 500 ms, or a rise of more than 60 ms from baseline, is the threshold that should make you look at the drug chart.

For pause-dependent torsades that recurs despite magnesium, raise the rate: overdrive pacing at 90-110 beats a minute or an isoprenaline infusion shortens the QT and abolishes the pauses that let the runs start.
cases.intro: The medics are still handing over a 52-year-old who has collapsed three times today when she stiffens on the trolley in front of you and her eyes roll back. The monitor fills with a wide, twisting rhythm whose amplitude winds up and down around the baseline. The strip the crew printed between her earlier episodes is in your hand: a long QT and ectopics falling on the T wave. This run is not stopping, and there is no pulse at the femoral.

speech.speaker: medic
speech.text: Third one today. The first two broke on their own in under a minute — this one's been going since we came through the door, and I can't feel a pulse.

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: That's not the usual wide complex — look at it twisting. No pulse. My hands are going on the chest.

cases.article: ATLS 11th Edition (2025) — Advanced Trauma Life Support: the xABCDE primary survey and damage-control resuscitation
cases.title: Stabbed in the groin
cases.chiefComplaint: 24M — stab wound to the right groin, bleeding through the dressing
cases.diagnosis: Exsanguinating haemorrhage from a stab wound to the right common femoral vessel
cases.context: 24-year-old man stabbed once in the right groin twelve minutes ago. A pressure dressing is on and has already soaked through twice; he is awake, frightened, tachycardic at 118 and 100 systolic and FALLING. True scenario is exsanguinating junctional arterial haemorrhage. CORRECT PATH (ATLS 11th edition, xABCDE): the x comes FIRST — a windlass tourniquet high and tight above the wound, or haemostatic wound packing with three minutes of uninterrupted direct pressure for a junctional wound that cannot be tourniqueted, BEFORE anyone looks at the airway. Then A and B (high-flow oxygen, his own patent airway), C (two large-bore cannulae or a humeral IO, type and crossmatch), damage-control resuscitation with a BALANCED 1:1:1 transfusion of red cells, plasma and platelets through a fluid warmer, TRANEXAMIC ACID 1 g IV inside the first ten minutes, permissive hypotension to a palpable radial pulse until surgical haemostasis, then D and E with aggressive rewarming to keep him above 36 degrees. Trauma and vascular surgery to the bedside, and definitive haemostasis in THEATRE, not in the CT scanner. RED HERRING: an initial haemoglobin that is still nearly normal, and the temptation to intubate a talking patient before the bleeding is controlled — induction on an uncontrolled bleed removes his sympathetic drive and arrests him. CRYSTALLOID-ONLY resuscitation lifts the pressure for five minutes, dilutes the clotting factors, cools him, and kills him. DETERIORATION: unchecked, the systolic slides 100 to 78 to 62 and he arrests in PEA at seven minutes; bleeding control halts the slide, and blood plus tranexamic acid converts him back to stable.
criticalActions: Control the exsanguinating haemorrhage first — tourniquet, wound packing or direct pressure BEFORE the airway (the x of xABCDE)
Get two large-bore IVs or intraosseous access and send a type and crossmatch
Activate the massive transfusion protocol and resuscitate with a balanced 1:1:1 ratio of red cells, plasma and platelets
Give tranexamic acid 1 g IV within the first ten minutes
Complete the rest of the primary survey — airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure — once the bleeding is controlled
Keep him warm and prevent the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy
Get trauma surgery and vascular surgery to the bedside for definitive repair
Take him to theatre for surgical haemostasis rather than to the CT scanner
learningPoints: ATLS 11th edition made the primary survey xABCDE: catastrophic external haemorrhage is controlled before the airway is assessed, because an open airway on an empty circulation delivers nothing.

A limb tourniquet goes 5-7 cm proximal to the wound and the windlass is turned until the bleeding STOPS — a half-tightened tourniquet occludes venous return only and bleeds faster. Write the time it went on.
A junctional wound at the groin has no thigh above it to tourniquet: pack the tract with haemostatic gauze and hold uninterrupted direct pressure for a full 3 minutes, or use a junctional tourniquet.

Resuscitate a bleeding patient with blood in a balanced 1:1:1 ratio of red cells to plasma to platelets; more than 1.5 L of crystalloid dilutes clotting factors, cools the patient and increases mortality.
Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours, given within 3 hours of injury — the survival benefit shrinks with every 15 minutes of delay, so give it inside the first ten.

Permissive hypotension — a systolic near 90 mmHg, or simply a palpable radial pulse — is the target until surgical haemostasis, with the exception of traumatic brain injury, where the systolic must stay above 110 mmHg.
Keep the patient above 36 degrees Celsius: hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy are the lethal triad, and clotting enzyme activity falls off a cliff below 35 degrees.
Replace ionised calcium after roughly every 4 units of citrated blood — calcium gluconate 3 g or calcium chloride 1 g — because citrate binds it and a heart with a calcium of 0.9 will not squeeze.
cases.intro: The medics come through the doors fast, one of them kneeling on the trolley with both hands pressed into a 24-year-old man's right groin. He is awake, grey, soaked to the knees in his own blood, and asking everyone who passes whether he is going to die. The dressing under the medic's hands is bright red and dripping onto the floor. The monitor reads 118 and 100 systolic.

speech.speaker: medic
speech.text: Stabbed outside a bar twelve minutes ago, one wound, right groin. It was pumping when we got there — I've had my hands on it the whole way in and it is still coming through.

speech.speaker: patient
speech.text: Am I going to die? Please — I can feel it running down my leg.

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: He's 118, 100 over 62, and the pressure is drifting. The blood fridge is ten steps away. Tell me what you want first.

cases.article: ATLS 11th Edition (2025) — Advanced Trauma Life Support: xABCDE, brain injury from the primary survey onward, and hypothermia as a primary-survey threat
cases.title: Head-on collision at speed
cases.chiefComplaint: 37F — restrained driver, high-speed head-on crash, twenty minutes trapped
cases.diagnosis: Multisystem blunt injury: left tension pneumothorax, unstable pelvic ring fracture with retroperitoneal bleeding, and moderate traumatic brain injury with a GCS of 9
cases.context: 37-year-old restrained driver of a car that hit another head-on at motorway speed; twenty minutes of extrication in the rain. THREE life threats are running at once. (1) A LEFT TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX — the SpO2 is 92 and falling, the left chest is quiet and getting hard to bag. (2) An UNSTABLE PELVIC RING with retroperitoneal bleeding — the systolic is 96 and falling — plus a degloved right thigh wound running freely onto the trolley. (3) A HEAD INJURY with a GCS of 9 (E2 V3 M4). CORRECT PATH (ATLS 11th edition, xABCDE): x FIRST — pack the thigh wound and hold pressure; then decompress the chest CLINICALLY, by finger thoracostomy or a needle at the 4th or 5th intercostal space in the anterior axillary line, WITHOUT waiting for a chest film; apply a pelvic binder at the level of the GREATER TROCHANTERS; balanced 1:1:1 massive transfusion with tranexamic acid 1 g; brain-directed care from the primary survey onward — GCS scored by component and repeated for TREND, head up 30 degrees, SpO2 above 94 percent, systolic above 110 mmHg, EtCO2 35 to 40 mmHg, NO prophylactic hyperventilation, hypertonic saline or mannitol only for signs of herniation; and active rewarming, because in ATLS 11 hypothermia belongs in the primary survey, not in the tidy-up. RED HERRING: sending an unstable patient to CT before the chest is decompressed and the pelvis is bound; waiting for a chest x-ray to confirm the tension; hyperventilating her 'for the head'. DETERIORATION: two clocks run in parallel — the saturations slide 92 to 86 to 78 to 66 and she arrests in PEA at seven and a half minutes unless the chest is decompressed, and the bleeding pelvis and thigh kill her at ten to fourteen minutes unless the wound is packed, the binder is on and blood is running. Missing either one kills her.
criticalActions: Control the external haemorrhage first — pack the bleeding thigh wound and hold direct pressure before you move to the airway (the x of xABCDE)
Decompress the tension pneumothorax on clinical grounds — finger or needle thoracostomy, without waiting for a chest x-ray
Apply a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters for the unstable pelvic ring
Activate the massive transfusion protocol at a 1:1:1 ratio and give tranexamic acid 1 g IV
Score the GCS by component and repeat it — the trend of the motor score is the alarm
Give brain-directed care: head up 30 degrees, EtCO2 35-40 mmHg, systolic above 110 mmHg, and hypertonic saline or mannitol only for herniation, never prophylactic hyperventilation
Prevent hypothermia actively — warmed blood and fluids, a forced-air warmer, and a core temperature above 36 degrees Celsius
Get trauma surgery, neurosurgery and orthopaedics involved, and move her to CT or theatre only once the chest and pelvis are treated
learningPoints: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis treated before imaging: a 5 cm needle at the 4th or 5th intercostal space in the anterior axillary line, which ATLS 11 prefers over the 2nd space mid-clavicular in adults, or better still a finger thoracostomy, which cannot kink or block.
ATLS 11th edition puts x before A: catastrophic external bleeding is packed or tourniqueted in the first seconds, because oxygen delivered into an empty circulation delivers nothing.

A pelvic binder goes at the level of the greater trochanters, not the iliac crests, and closes an open-book pelvis; apply it once, leave it on until definitive fixation, and never spring the pelvis repeatedly.

Score the GCS by its three components and by its trend — E2 V3 M4 is a very different patient from E1 V1 M7 at the same total of 9, and a motor score falling by 2 points is an expanding mass lesion until a CT says otherwise.

Secondary brain injury is prevented by numbers: SpO2 above 94 percent, systolic above 110 mmHg, EtCO2 35-40 mmHg, head up 30 degrees, and glucose kept normal. A single episode of hypotension roughly doubles mortality in traumatic brain injury.

Prophylactic hyperventilation is harmful: it constricts cerebral vessels and causes ischaemia. Drop the EtCO2 to 30-35 mmHg only as a short bridge for signs of herniation — a blown pupil, extensor posturing, a Cushing response — while osmotherapy is drawn up.

For herniation give 3% hypertonic saline 250 mL or 23.4% saline 30 mL, or mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg; prefer hypertonic saline in a bleeding patient, because mannitol is an osmotic diuretic and will drop a borderline blood pressure.

Hypothermia belongs in the primary survey: below 35 degrees Celsius the clotting cascade enzymes slow markedly and the coagulopathy of trauma accelerates. Warm the room, the fluids and the blood, and cover her the moment she is exposed.
cases.intro: The trolley comes in with a firefighter still holding a scoop under it and a medic squeezing a bag. A 37-year-old woman, restrained driver of a car that hit another head-on at motorway speed, twenty minutes to cut her out in the rain. She is not talking. Her right thigh is degloved and running onto the sheet, her left chest is barely moving, and the monitor reads 124, 96 systolic, saturations of 92 and a temperature of 35.1.

speech.speaker: medic
speech.text: Head-on, both cars written off, about sixty miles an hour. Restrained driver, twenty minutes trapped. She was talking to us through the window at the start and she stopped about ten minutes ago.

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: Sats 92 on fifteen litres and she is getting harder to bag. Pressure 96, and there is blood pouring off the end of the trolley from her thigh. She is freezing.

speech.speaker: family
speech.text: I'm her sister — I was in the car behind. Please, is she breathing?

cases.article: ATLS 11th Edition (2025) — Advanced Trauma Life Support: traumatic cardiac arrest and the trauma-specific reversible causes
cases.title: Crushed under machinery
cases.chiefComplaint: 30M — crushed under a pallet press at work, CPR in progress on arrival
cases.diagnosis: Traumatic cardiac arrest from a crush mechanism: bilateral tension pneumothoraces, exsanguinating limb haemorrhage and hyperkalaemia
cases.context: 30-year-old warehouse worker pinned across the chest and left leg under a pallet press for eighteen minutes. He was conscious and talking to his workmates while trapped and arrested as the machine was lifted off him — the classic reperfusion arrest of a crush mechanism. He arrives PULSELESS in PEA with the medics bagging and compressing. True scenario is TRAUMATIC cardiac arrest, and the algorithm is NOT the medical one. CORRECT PATH (ATLS 11th edition): fix the cause in the first three to four minutes — BILATERAL FINGER THORACOSTOMY (both chests are silent and rigid, and you cannot auscultate a tension over compressions), EXTERNAL HAEMORRHAGE CONTROL with a tourniquet on the degloved left thigh, and BLOOD, 1:1:1 through a rapid infuser, not crystalloid. Oxygenate and ventilate with a definitive airway confirmed by waveform capnography. Look at the subxiphoid view during the pulse check for tamponade and consider a resuscitative thoracotomy. Anticipate CRUSH SYNDROME — the potassium is 6.9 — and treat it with calcium, insulin and dextrose, and salbutamol. ROSC comes at the next rhythm check once the chests are decompressed AND blood is running. RED HERRING: reaching for EPINEPHRINE first. It is accepted here and it is the wrong first move: a vasopressor squeezes an empty heart, and the minute spent drawing it up is the minute the thoracostomy needed. Crystalloid instead of blood is the other trap. DETERIORATION: untreated PEA degrades to asystole at eight minutes and the resuscitation is over at twenty.
criticalActions: Stop the external bleeding first — tourniquet the crushed leg and pack what cannot be tourniqueted, before drugs or the airway (the x of xABCDE)
Decompress both sides of the chest immediately — bilateral finger thoracostomy, without waiting for a chest film
Transfuse blood rather than crystalloid — activate the massive transfusion protocol and run 1:1:1 through a rapid infuser
Oxygenate and ventilate — secure the airway and confirm it with waveform capnography
Work the reversible causes specific to trauma — hypovolaemia, tension pneumothorax, tamponade and hypoxia — instead of reaching for epinephrine first
Look for tamponade on the subxiphoid view at the pulse check and consider a resuscitative thoracotomy
Anticipate crush syndrome — check the potassium, treat hyperkalaemia with calcium, insulin and dextrose, and send a creatine kinase
Once he has a pulse, take him straight to theatre for definitive haemorrhage control
learningPoints: Traumatic cardiac arrest is not medical arrest: the four fixes are external haemorrhage control, bilateral thoracostomy, blood, and oxygenation, all inside the first three to four minutes. Epinephrine on an empty heart squeezes nothing.

Bilateral finger thoracostomy at the 4th or 5th intercostal space in the anterior axillary line takes about 30 seconds a side and treats a tension pneumothorax you can neither hear nor percuss over running compressions.
Chest compressions do far less in hypovolaemic traumatic arrest than filling the heart does — never let compressions delay thoracostomy or transfusion, and never let the code become a medical one.
Give blood, not saline: 1:1:1 red cells, plasma and platelets, warmed, with tranexamic acid 1 g IV. A litre of crystalloid dilutes clot, drops the temperature and buys nothing.

Resuscitative thoracotomy is for penetrating chest arrest with signs of life within about 15 minutes, or blunt arrest with under 10 minutes of CPR — to release tamponade, control hilar bleeding and cross-clamp the aorta.

Crush injury releases potassium from dying muscle: treat a hyperkalaemic arrest with calcium chloride 1 g (or calcium gluconate 3 g) IV, then insulin 10 units with 25 g of dextrose, plus nebulised salbutamol, and send a creatine kinase.
EtCO2 during CPR is the honest number: under 10 mmHg means the compressions or the filling are inadequate, and an abrupt rise above 35 mmHg announces ROSC before anyone feels a pulse.
Keep him above 36 degrees Celsius throughout — a cold trauma patient does not clot, and the coagulopathy is what kills the ones who survive the first ten minutes.
cases.intro: Two medics come through the doors with one of them up on the trolley doing compressions and the other squeezing a bag. A 30-year-old warehouse worker was pinned under a pallet press for eighteen minutes; he was talking to his workmates the whole time they were lifting it, and he arrested the moment the weight came off. The monitor shows slow, wide, organised complexes and there is no pulse to go with them. His left thigh is degloved and still running onto the trolley sheet.

speech.speaker: medic
speech.text: Crushed across the chest and the left leg, pinned about eighteen minutes. He was awake and talking the whole time. Went off as soon as they lifted it — those same slow wide complexes from the start, and we never shocked him. Eleven minutes of CPR, no adrenaline given.

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: No pulse, no pressure. EtCO2 is nine. Compressions are running. What do you want first, doctor?

cases.article: AHA 2025 Guidelines for CPR and ECC — Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS)
cases.title: Collapse at a Little League game
cases.chiefComplaint: 7-year-old boy, 24 kg, struck in the chest by a batted ball and collapsed, CPR in progress
cases.diagnosis: Ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest from commotio cordis (blunt precordial blow)
cases.context: Theo, 7 years old, WEIGHT 24 KG. A line drive hit him square on the sternum at a Little League game; he took two steps and dropped. His father started compressions within a minute and the first analysed rhythm was VENTRICULAR FIBRILLATION. No shock has been delivered. He has no medical history, takes nothing, and his heart was normal ten minutes ago. TRUE SCENARIO: commotio cordis — a structurally normal heart thrown into fibrillation by an impact landing on the upstroke of the T wave. CORRECT PATH: compressions that barely stop, DEFIBRILLATION at 2 J/kg (48 J) at once and 4 J/kg (96 J) thereafter up to 10 J/kg, EPINEPHRINE 0.01 mg/kg = 0.24 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes, AMIODARONE 5 mg/kg = 120 mg (or lidocaine 1 mg/kg) for fibrillation that survives the shocks, an airway with WAVEFORM CAPNOGRAPHY, and CPR quality judged on EtCO2 together with the ARTERIAL DIASTOLIC PRESSURE (target at least 30 mmHg in a child). Both parents are at the bedside and are asking to stay — family presence during resuscitation is part of the care, not a distraction. RED HERRINGS: adult joules and the adult 1 mg epinephrine ampoule; hunting a cardiac history that does not exist; asking the family to leave. DETERIORATION: untreated fibrillation goes fine, then flat.
criticalActions: Run high-quality compressions at 100-120 a minute, one third of the chest depth, with minimal interruptions
Defibrillate the shockable rhythm immediately at 2 J/kg — 48 J for 24 kg
Escalate to 4 J/kg (96 J) for the second and later shocks, up to 10 J/kg or the adult dose
Give epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg — 0.24 mg IV/IO — and repeat it every 3-5 minutes
Give amiodarone 5 mg/kg (120 mg) or lidocaine 1 mg/kg for fibrillation that persists after the shocks
Secure the airway and judge CPR quality on waveform capnography and the arterial diastolic pressure
Keep the parents at the bedside with one named team member assigned to them
After ROSC get a 12-lead and an echocardiogram and admit to the paediatric intensive care unit
learningPoints: Paediatric defibrillation is weight-based: 2 J/kg for the first shock, 4 J/kg for the second, then up to 10 J/kg or the adult dose — for a 24 kg child that is 48 J, then 96 J.

Epinephrine in paediatric arrest is 0.01 mg/kg IV/IO (0.1 mL/kg of 1:10,000) to a maximum of 1 mg every 3-5 minutes; a 24 kg child gets 0.24 mg, and the adult ampoule off the shelf is four times that.
Amiodarone 5 mg/kg IV/IO, repeatable to a total of 15 mg/kg, or lidocaine 1 mg/kg, for VF or pulseless VT that survives the first shocks.

AHA 2025 asks you to judge CPR quality on EtCO2 AND the arterial diastolic pressure — aim for a diastolic of at least 30 mmHg in a child and at least 25 mmHg in an infant, and fix your compressions if you are under it.

Commotio cordis is a normal heart fibrillating because a blow landed in a 20-millisecond window on the T wave upstroke; the only treatment is a fast shock, and survival tracks almost entirely with the time to it.

Parents who stay for their child's resuscitation cope better afterwards and disrupt the team less than teams expect — offer them a place at the head of the bed and one staff member whose only job is them.
cases.intro: The medics come through the doors doing compressions on a seven-year-old still in his baseball uniform. He took a batted ball square on the chest, walked two steps and went down; a parent in the stands had hands on him inside a minute. The monitor shows a coarse, chaotic trace with no organised complexes, and nobody has shocked him yet. His mother and father are right behind the stretcher.

speech.speaker: medic
speech.text: Theo, seven years old, twenty-four kilos. Batted ball to the chest, collapsed straight away, dad had compressions going in under a minute. Same trace from the moment we had pads on him, and we have not shocked him.

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: Twenty-four kilos, doctor — two joules per kilo is forty-eight. Paediatric pads are on, defibrillator's charged, I'm on the chest.

speech.speaker: family
speech.text: That's our son. He was fine, he was batting — please, we're not leaving him.

cases.article: AHA 2025 Guidelines for CPR and ECC — Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS)
cases.title: Two days of noisy breathing, now barely rousable
cases.chiefComplaint: 3-year-old girl, 14 kg, two days of a harsh barking cough, now mottled and hard to wake
cases.diagnosis: Hypoxic bradycardia from upper airway obstruction in severe croup — pre-arrest, not yet arrested
cases.context: Ruby, 3 years old, WEIGHT 14 KG. Two days of a barking cough and stridor that her parents were managing at home; this morning she went quiet. She arrives mottled to the shoulders, barely rousable, HR 48, BP 74/40, SpO2 84% on room air, minimal air entry and no audible stridor because she has stopped moving enough air to make one. SHE IS NOT ARRESTED. TRUE SCENARIO: hypoxic bradycardia — the commonest bradycardia in a child and a pre-arrest sign, not a conduction problem. CORRECT PATH: open the airway and give EFFECTIVE BAG-MASK VENTILATION with 100% oxygen; reassess the heart rate after 30 seconds of it; START COMPRESSIONS if the rate stays under 60 with poor perfusion DESPITE adequate oxygenation and ventilation; get IO or IV access; EPINEPHRINE 0.01 mg/kg = 0.14 mg IV/IO only after oxygenation, ventilation and compressions; then treat the obstruction itself with nebulised epinephrine and dexamethasone. RED HERRINGS: atropine first (this is not vagal and not a primary block), epinephrine first, transcutaneous pacing, and intubating a swollen subglottis before trying to ventilate with a mask. DETERIORATION: unventilated, the rate falls, she loses her pulse into PEA and then asystole.
criticalActions: Open the airway and give effective bag-mask ventilation with 100% oxygen before reaching for any drug
Reassess the heart rate and perfusion after 30 seconds of effective ventilation
Start chest compressions if the heart rate stays under 60 with poor perfusion despite adequate oxygenation and ventilation
Establish IO or IV access
Give epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg — 0.14 mg IV/IO — for bradycardia that persists after oxygenation, ventilation and compressions
Name the bradycardia as hypoxic rather than vagal or a primary block — atropine and pacing belong to those, not to this
Treat the upper airway obstruction itself with nebulised epinephrine and dexamethasone
Admit to the paediatric intensive care unit with the airway team aware
learningPoints: Bradycardia in a child is hypoxic until proven otherwise: the treatment is oxygen and effective ventilation, and a heart rate that climbs with bagging has told you the diagnosis.
Start chest compressions when the heart rate is under 60 with poor perfusion DESPITE adequate oxygenation and ventilation — a rate of 48 in a child nobody is ventilating needs a bag first, not hands.
Paediatric epinephrine is 0.01 mg/kg IV/IO (max 1 mg) every 3-5 minutes — 0.14 mg in a 14 kg child; the adult 1 mg ampoule is a seven-fold overdose here.

Atropine is 0.02 mg/kg IV/IO (maximum single dose 0.5 mg) and belongs to vagally mediated bradycardia and primary AV block; given for hypoxic bradycardia it wastes the minute that ventilation would have used.
AHA 2025 grades CPR quality on EtCO2 and the arterial diastolic pressure together — at least 25 mmHg diastolic in an infant and 30 mmHg in a child.

Croup that has gone quiet is not better: stridor disappears when the child stops moving air. Nebulised epinephrine 0.5 mL/kg of 1:1000 (max 5 mL) and dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg buy hours, but only once someone is ventilating her.
cases.intro: A three-year-old is carried in by her father, floppy over his forearm. She has had a barking cough for two days; this morning the noise stopped and she stopped waking properly. She is mottled to the shoulders, her chest is barely moving, and the monitor picks up a heart rate of 48 with saturations of 84%. She still has a pulse.

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: Ruby, three, fourteen kilos — I've written it on the board. Rate's 48, sats 84, and she's grey. She's not arrested, doctor, but she's close.

speech.speaker: family
speech.text: She was barking like a seal all night. Then this morning she went quiet and I thought she was finally sleeping.

cases.article: AHA 2025 Guidelines for CPR and ECC — Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS)
cases.title: Four-month-old off her feeds and grey
cases.chiefComplaint: 4-month-old girl, 6 kg, a day of poor feeding, now grey, sweaty and breathing fast
cases.diagnosis: Supraventricular tachycardia with poor perfusion and early heart failure in a 4-month-old
cases.context: Nina, 4 months old, WEIGHT 6 KG. A day of taking half her feeds, sweating on the bottle, and this morning grey and breathing hard. Monitor shows a NARROW-COMPLEX TACHYCARDIA at 240 that does not vary beat to beat, BP 62/38, cool mottled legs, cap refill four seconds, and a liver edge three centimetres below the costal margin. She is afebrile and there is no diarrhoea, no blood loss and no story that explains a rate of 240. TRUE SCENARIO: SVT with poor perfusion. CORRECT PATH: distinguish SVT from SINUS TACHYCARDIA (rate above 220 in an infant, absolutely fixed, no P waves, no history that explains it); get a 12-lead and keep a rhythm strip running; VAGAL MANOEUVRE with ice water to the face while access is obtained; ADENOSINE 0.1 mg/kg = 0.6 mg by rapid push with an immediate flush, then 0.2 mg/kg = 1.2 mg; SYNCHRONIZED CARDIOVERSION 0.5-1 J/kg = 3-6 J then 2 J/kg = 12 J if she deteriorates or adenosine fails. RED HERRINGS: treating her as septic or dehydrated and giving fluid for a sinus tachycardia she does not have; verapamil (arrest risk in infants); an unsynchronized shock; adult adenosine doses of 6 and 12 mg. DETERIORATION: an untreated infant at 240 fails and arrests into PEA.
criticalActions: Call it SVT rather than sinus tachycardia — a fixed rate above 220 in an infant with no history that explains it
Get a 12-lead ECG and keep a continuous rhythm strip running through every intervention
Try a vagal manoeuvre — ice water to the face — without letting it delay drug treatment
Get IV or IO access in the most proximal vein you can reach
Give adenosine 0.1 mg/kg (0.6 mg) by rapid push with an immediate flush, then 0.2 mg/kg (1.2 mg)
Move to synchronized cardioversion at 0.5-1 J/kg (3-6 J), then 2 J/kg (12 J), if she deteriorates or adenosine fails
Avoid verapamil and avoid an unsynchronized shock in an infant with a pulse
Admit for cardiology review, an echocardiogram and a plan for the next episode
learningPoints: Sinus tachycardia in an infant tops out near 220 and wanders beat to beat with handling, fever and pain; a rate above 220 that never varies, with no visible P waves and no history to explain it, is SVT.

Adenosine is 0.1 mg/kg to a maximum of 6 mg first, then 0.2 mg/kg to a maximum of 12 mg — 0.6 mg then 1.2 mg in a 6 kg infant — pushed fast into the most proximal vein with an instant flush and the strip running.
Synchronized cardioversion for unstable SVT is 0.5-1 J/kg escalating to 2 J/kg: 3 to 6 J then 12 J in a 6 kg infant. An adult setting of 120 J is twenty times the starting dose.

The infant vagal manoeuvre is ice water to the face — a bag of iced water over the forehead, eyes and bridge of the nose for up to 15 seconds. Never press on the eyeballs and never massage both carotids.
A liver edge pushed below the costal margin, a gallop and cool peripheries in an infant with a fixed tachycardia is heart failure caused by the rate; treat the rhythm and the failure follows it.
Verapamil can cause refractory hypotension and cardiac arrest in infants and has no place here; if adenosine fails and she is unstable, cardiovert her.
cases.intro: A four-month-old is handed to you off her mother's shoulder. She has been taking half her feeds for a day, sweating through them, and this morning she went grey. She is breathing fast, her legs are cool and mottled to the knee, and the monitor reads a narrow tachycardia at 240 that does not move.

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: Nina, four months, six kilos — six kilos, doctor, everything is going to be a fraction. Rate's locked at 240, pressure 62 over 38, she's cold to the knees.

speech.speaker: family
speech.text: She wouldn't finish a bottle yesterday and she's been sweaty every time I feed her. This morning she just looked wrong.

cases.article: AHA 2025 Guidelines for CPR and ECC — Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS)
cases.title: Silent chest in a struggling five-year-old
cases.chiefComplaint: 5-year-old boy, 18 kg, brought in fighting for breath, now exhausted and quiet
cases.diagnosis: Status asthmaticus with respiratory arrest progressing to PEA cardiac arrest and a tension pneumothorax from dynamic hyperinflation
cases.context: Owen, 5 years old, WEIGHT 18 KG. Three days of a cold, then a night of worsening wheeze; ten salbutamol puffs at home did nothing. He arrives sitting forward, tripoding, speaking in single words, sats 85% on a mask, and within a few minutes he is quiet — silent chest, minimal effort, drowsy. TRUE SCENARIO: status asthmaticus with respiratory arrest that progresses to PEA, complicated by dynamic hyperinflation and a right tension pneumothorax once positive pressure starts. CORRECT PATH: continuous nebulised salbutamol with ipratropium and oxygen; systemic steroid early (methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg = 36 mg IV) and MAGNESIUM SULFATE 50 mg/kg = 900 mg IV over 20 minutes; ventilate at a low rate with a LONG EXPIRATORY TIME; when the pulse goes, compressions and the PEA algorithm with EPINEPHRINE 0.01 mg/kg = 0.18 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes; a FLUID BOLUS 20 mL/kg = 360 mL for the obstructive shock; DISCONNECT THE CIRCUIT and press the chest to release stacked breaths; NEEDLE DECOMPRESSION and then a finger thoracostomy or chest tube for the tension pneumothorax. RED HERRINGS: bagging him hard and fast (it is what causes the arrest); repeated epinephrine while the chest is hyperinflated and undecompressed; blaming the arrest on the drugs. DETERIORATION: unrecognised air trapping turns PEA into asystole.
criticalActions: Give continuous nebulised salbutamol with ipratropium and high-flow oxygen from the first minute
Give a systemic steroid early and magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (900 mg) IV over 20 minutes
Ventilate at a low rate with a long expiratory time and disconnect the circuit to let a hyperinflated chest deflate
Start compressions and run the PEA algorithm the moment he loses his pulse
Give epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg — 0.18 mg IV/IO — every 3-5 minutes
Give a fluid bolus of 20 mL/kg (360 mL) for the obstructive shock of hyperinflation
Decompress a tension pneumothorax with a needle and then a finger thoracostomy or chest tube
Admit to the paediatric intensive care unit after ROSC
learningPoints: Paediatric arrest almost always arrives through the lungs: a child who stops breathing arrests within minutes, so the airway and the ventilation are the resuscitation and the compressions are what you do because you were late.

In a ventilated asthmatic, hyperinflation is the enemy — 8 to 10 breaths a minute, short inspiration, long expiration; if the pressure climbs and the pulse fades, disconnect the circuit and press on the chest to let the air out.

Sudden loss of output when positive pressure starts in asthma is breath stacking or a tension pneumothorax until proven otherwise; decompress the chest before you reach for another round of epinephrine.
Epinephrine in paediatric arrest is 0.01 mg/kg IV/IO (max 1 mg) every 3-5 minutes — 0.18 mg in an 18 kg child.
Magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg IV (maximum 2 g) over 20 minutes is the escalation for severe asthma that is not answering continuous beta agonist and steroid.

AHA 2025: judge CPR quality on EtCO2 and on the arterial diastolic pressure — a diastolic of at least 30 mmHg in a child, 25 mmHg in an infant, tells you the compressions are generating coronary perfusion.
cases.intro: A five-year-old is carried in sitting bolt upright on his mother's arm, shoulders up around his ears, answering you one word at a time. Ten puffs at home did nothing. His saturations are 85% on a mask and, in the two minutes it takes to get him onto the trolley, the wheeze you could hear from the corridor stops — and so does most of his effort.

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: Owen, five, eighteen kilos. Sats 85 on a mask, rate 168. He was wheezing when we put him on the bed and now I can't hear anything at all.

speech.speaker: family
speech.text: He's had his inhaler ten times since two this morning. He kept saying he couldn't get it in and now he's stopped saying anything.

cases.article: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines for CPR and ECC — Neonatal Resuscitation
cases.title: Newborn limp at delivery
cases.chiefComplaint: Newborn at 39 weeks — handed over floppy, no breathing effort, heart rate 50
cases.diagnosis: Perinatal asphyxia with secondary apnea of the newborn, needing ventilation, chest compressions and epinephrine
cases.context: A 39-week male, 3.4 kg, delivered vaginally after a second stage that ran close to three hours with late decelerations for the last twenty minutes. The fluid was clear. The cord was clamped at 65 seconds because he came out with no tone. He is apneic on the warmer with a heart rate of about 50 at the base of the cord. CORRECT PATH: the initial steps in the first 30 seconds — warm, dry, stimulate, position the airway — then POSITIVE-PRESSURE VENTILATION at 40 to 60 breaths a minute inside the Golden Minute because he is apneic with a rate under 100. The chest does not rise on the first attempt, so MR SOPA (mask adjust, reposition, suction, open mouth, pressure up, alternative airway) is the corrective sequence. His rate stays under 60 after 30 seconds of ventilation that is actually moving the chest, so CHEST COMPRESSIONS 3:1 with ventilation (90 compressions and 30 breaths a minute) and an ADVANCED AIRWAY. Then an UMBILICAL VENOUS CATHETER and EPINEPHRINE 0.02 mg/kg (0.068 mg) IV, reassessing the heart rate every 30 seconds until it is over 100. RED HERRING: reaching for drugs, suction or a tube before anyone has moved air — nothing in newborn resuscitation works until the lungs are inflated. DETERIORATION: without effective ventilation the heart rate falls from 50 through the 30s and 20s to nothing.
criticalActions: Warm, dry, stimulate and position the newborn in the first 30 seconds of life
Start positive-pressure ventilation at 40 to 60 breaths a minute inside the Golden Minute
Run the MR SOPA corrective steps when the chest does not rise with ventilation
Start chest compressions at 3:1 with ventilation once the heart rate stays under 60 after 30 seconds of effective ventilation
Place an advanced airway — an endotracheal tube or a laryngeal mask — when compressions begin
Place an umbilical venous catheter for emergency vascular access
Give epinephrine 0.02 mg/kg (0.068 mg) IV and repeat every 3 to 5 minutes while the heart rate stays under 60
Reassess the heart rate every 30 seconds and hand over to the neonatal team for post-resuscitation care
learningPoints: The Golden Minute: warm, dry, stimulate and position in the first 30 seconds, and have positive-pressure ventilation running by 60 seconds of life if the baby is apneic or gasping or the heart rate is under 100.
Heart rate is the measure of a newborn resuscitation. Ventilation at 40 to 60 breaths a minute is the intervention that changes it — a rising rate is the proof that the lungs are being inflated.
When the chest does not rise, run MR SOPA in order: mask adjust, reposition the head, suction the mouth and nose, open the mouth, increase the inflation pressure, then an alternative airway.

A heart rate under 60 after 30 seconds of ventilation that visibly moves the chest calls for chest compressions at 3:1 with ventilation — 90 compressions and 30 breaths a minute — with an advanced airway and 100% oxygen.

Epinephrine is 0.02 mg/kg IV (an acceptable range of 0.01 to 0.03 mg/kg), preferably through an umbilical venous catheter; the endotracheal route at 0.05 to 0.1 mg/kg is only a stopgap while access is being obtained.
AHA/AAP 2025: delay cord clamping for at least 60 seconds in vigorous term and preterm newborns, and consider intact-cord milking for non-vigorous newborns of 35 to 42 weeks.

AHA/AAP 2025 recognise video laryngoscopy as a tool for neonatal intubation, and the laryngeal mask as the answer when face-mask ventilation fails — in some settings it is a reasonable first-line airway. These are the first neonatal guidelines written jointly by the AHA and the AAP.
cases.intro: Obstetrics calls you into room 4 for a delivery at 39 weeks after a second stage that ran nearly three hours. The fluid was clear. The baby comes to the warmer limp and blue, no cry, no chest movement, and the nurse with two fingers on the base of the cord is counting a rate around 50. The warmer clock is already running.

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: Thirty-nine weeks, three point four kilos. He came out floppy, no cry, no effort at all. I'm counting about fifty at the cord.

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: Warmer's on, towels are here, the bag and mask are at your right hand. Tell me what you want.

speech.speaker: family
speech.text: Why isn't he crying? Somebody please tell me why he isn't crying.

cases.article: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines for CPR and ECC — Neonatal Resuscitation
cases.title: Non-vigorous newborn at delivery
cases.chiefComplaint: Newborn at 40 weeks — thick stained fluid, limp with no respiratory effort, heart rate 70
cases.diagnosis: Respiratory depression in a non-vigorous newborn born through thick meconium-stained amniotic fluid
cases.context: A 40+2 week female, 3.6 kg, delivered vaginally through thick particulate meconium noticed at rupture two hours before delivery. She is non-vigorous: limp, no respiratory effort, heart rate about 70. The cord was clamped at 30 seconds because she was flat. CORRECT PATH: warm, dry, position and stimulate briefly, then POSITIVE-PRESSURE VENTILATION inside the Golden Minute — she is apneic with a heart rate under 100. Clear the mouth and nose only if secretions are obstructing. Reassess the heart rate after 30 seconds of ventilation and keep going until it is over 100 with spontaneous breathing, then monitor preductal saturation on the RIGHT hand and titrate oxygen to the minute-specific target. RED HERRING: intubating a non-vigorous meconium-stained newborn to suction the trachea. The 2025 AHA/AAP guidelines do not recommend routine tracheal suctioning — it delays the one thing that works, and deep suction can drop the heart rate further by a vagal reflex. Intubation belongs here only if MR SOPA fails to move the chest, which points to real airway obstruction. DETERIORATION: while nobody ventilates, the heart rate slides from 70 through the 50s and 30s to arrest.
criticalActions: Warm, dry, position and briefly stimulate the newborn without delaying ventilation
Start positive-pressure ventilation inside the Golden Minute for a non-vigorous newborn with no respiratory effort and a heart rate under 100
Choose immediate ventilation over routine tracheal suctioning in a non-vigorous meconium-stained newborn
Reassess the heart rate after 30 seconds of ventilation and continue until it is over 100
Run MR SOPA and reach for intubation or a laryngeal mask only if the chest still does not rise
Put the pulse oximeter on the right hand and titrate oxygen to the minute-specific preductal target
Check the temperature and the blood glucose and hand over to the neonatal team for observation
learningPoints: AHA/AAP 2025: routine intubation for tracheal suctioning of a non-vigorous meconium-stained newborn is no longer recommended — start positive-pressure ventilation instead, because inflating the lungs is what raises the heart rate.
Non-vigorous means poor tone, poor respiratory effort or a heart rate under 100. Any one of them, with meconium or without it, buys the same answer: ventilation inside the Golden Minute.
Deep tracheal suction stimulates a vagal reflex and can drop an already slow newborn heart rate — suction only what is obstructing the airway, using the mouth and then the nose.

Reassess the heart rate every 30 seconds. Rising above 100 with spontaneous breathing is the signal to stop ventilating; staying under 60 after 30 seconds of chest-moving ventilation is the signal to start compressions at 3:1.

Intubation in this baby is reserved for airway obstruction that MR SOPA does not fix, or for compressions. Video laryngoscopy is a recognised tool and a laryngeal mask is an accepted rescue when the face mask fails.

Preductal saturation is measured on the RIGHT hand, and the targets climb with the clock: 60 to 65% at one minute, 70 to 75% at three minutes, 80 to 85% at five minutes and 85 to 95% by ten minutes. Start ventilation in room air at term.
AHA/AAP 2025: delay cord clamping at least 60 seconds in a vigorous newborn, and consider intact-cord milking rather than immediate clamping in a non-vigorous newborn of 35 to 42 weeks.
cases.intro: You are called to a delivery at 40 weeks where the fluid went thick and green two hours ago. The baby is put on the warmer stained head to foot, limp, with no respiratory effort and no cry. The nurse has her stethoscope on the chest and calls a heart rate of 70. Somebody has already reached for the laryngoscope on the assumption that you will want to suction her out.

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: Forty weeks and two days, three point six kilos. Thick meconium since rupture. She's limp, no effort, heart rate seventy.

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: Blade and a meconium aspirator are open on the tray. Do you want me to set you up to suction her, or do you want something else first?

speech.speaker: family
speech.text: The midwife said the water was green. Is that what's wrong with her?

cases.article: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines for CPR and ECC — Neonatal Resuscitation
cases.title: Newborn pale at delivery
cases.chiefComplaint: Newborn at 38 weeks — born white and floppy after a sudden bleed in labor, heart rate 40
cases.diagnosis: Hypovolemic shock in the newborn from acute placental abruption
cases.context: A 38-week female, 3.1 kg, delivered by category-1 caesarean 14 minutes after the mother presented with abdominal pain, a rigid uterus and vaginal bleeding. There was a large retroplacental clot. The baby is white rather than blue, profoundly floppy, apneic, with a heart rate of 40 and pulses you cannot feel. CORRECT PATH: initial steps, then POSITIVE-PRESSURE VENTILATION immediately, CHEST COMPRESSIONS at 3:1 for a rate under 60, an ADVANCED AIRWAY, an UMBILICAL VENOUS CATHETER and EPINEPHRINE 0.02 mg/kg (0.062 mg) IV. The heart rate will not come up on any of it, and that is the point: a newborn who fails the algorithm has a cause. Here it is blood loss, and the treatment is VOLUME — 10 mL/kg (31 mL) of O-negative blood or normal saline over 5 to 10 minutes, repeated if needed. RED HERRING: more epinephrine, more pressure, another tube. Pallor that does not pink up with good ventilation, a persistently slow rate and absent pulses are hypovolemia until proven otherwise. DETERIORATION: without volume the heart rate never recovers and the baby arrests.
criticalActions: Warm, dry, stimulate and position the newborn within the first 30 seconds
Start positive-pressure ventilation immediately for an apneic newborn with a heart rate under 100
Start chest compressions at 3:1 with ventilation for a heart rate under 60 after 30 seconds of effective ventilation
Place an advanced airway and confirm it while compressions continue
Place an umbilical venous catheter for emergency vascular access
Give epinephrine 0.02 mg/kg (0.062 mg) IV and repeat every 3 to 5 minutes while the heart rate is under 60
Recognise hypovolemia when the heart rate does not respond and give 10 mL/kg (31 mL) of O-negative blood or normal saline over 5 to 10 minutes
Send a blood gas, a hemoglobin and a glucose, and hand over to the neonatal team
learningPoints: A newborn who does not respond to effective ventilation, compressions and epinephrine has a cause — think hypovolemia, pneumothorax, a blocked or displaced tube, and congenital airway or heart disease.
Volume for the newborn is 10 mL/kg of O-negative blood or normal saline given over 5 to 10 minutes, repeated if the response is incomplete. In acute blood loss, blood is the better fluid.

Pallor rather than cyanosis, a heart rate that stays slow on good ventilation, weak or absent pulses and a poor response to epinephrine are the signature of acute blood loss at delivery — abruption, vasa praevia, cord accident or feto-maternal hemorrhage.
Epinephrine is 0.02 mg/kg IV (range 0.01 to 0.03 mg/kg) every 3 to 5 minutes while the heart rate stays under 60, preferably through an umbilical venous catheter placed 4 to 5 cm for emergency use.
Compressions are 3:1 with ventilation — 90 compressions and 30 breaths a minute — with the two-thumb encircling technique, one third of the chest depth, and 100% oxygen once compressions start.

AHA/AAP 2025: delay cord clamping at least 60 seconds in vigorous term and preterm newborns; for a non-vigorous newborn of 35 to 42 weeks, intact-cord milking may be considered, and it is one of the few ways to give an acutely bled newborn some of its own blood back.

A cord arterial pH under 7.0 with a base deficit of 12 mmol/L or more marks significant acidemia and, with an abnormal neurological examination at 36 weeks or more, opens the six-hour window for therapeutic hypothermia at 33.5 degrees for 72 hours.
cases.intro: A category-1 caesarean at 38 weeks for abdominal pain, a woody uterus and heavy vaginal bleeding. Fourteen minutes from the decision to the delivery. The obstetrician lifts out a baby who is white rather than blue, completely floppy, not breathing, and hands her to you. The nurse has a stethoscope on the chest and says forty. There is a large clot on the back of the placenta in the kidney dish.

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: Thirty-eight weeks, three point one kilos. Heart rate forty and I can't feel a pulse anywhere. She's white, not blue.

speech.speaker: consultant
speech.text: Obstetrics — there was a big retroplacental clot, easily a third of the placental bed. She has lost blood.

speech.speaker: nurse
speech.text: Warmer's ready, mask is on the circuit, and the blood bank has O-negative in the fridge on this floor.
